extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in disinformation, propaganda, and media manipulation
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia overview that defines 'information laundering', describes how illegitimate or false information is moved from fringe/unverified sources into mainstream discourse, gives examples, outlines mechanisms (bots, deepfakes, state actors, AI), and notes related concepts and detection efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and attribution transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The surfacing of news, false or otherwise, from unverified sources into the mainstream; when reputable news organizations report on something a blog or low-credibility platform has written and later coverage omits the original source, the assertion is 'laundered' and gains credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jon Stewart's summary: a piece attributed to an original source gains credibility when subsequent coverage omits origin. Example: a blog post is cited by a reputable outlet, then other outlets drop the attribution and treat the claim as trusted information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow through social networks and intermediary sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Illegitimate exchanges of information flow through social networks, political blogs, and search engines where they intermix with mainstream ideas and are gradually washed of their radical origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adam Klein's theory: conspiracies incubate on platforms like Reddit or Twitter, then ‘graduate’ onto more respected websites and political blogs before being picked up by mainstream news outlets as 'trusted information.' Tracking the chain of reposting and republishing is key to detecting laundering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduation from fringe to mainstream (chain escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern where content moves from fringe communities to respected sites and finally to mainstream outlets, increasing perceived legitimacy at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for an originating post in niche forums or blogs followed by amplification on progressively more prominent sites; the omission or obfuscation of the original source at later stages is a hallmark of laundering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of manipulated media (deepfakes, photo/video manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faked videos (deepfakes) and images (photograph manipulation) create media moments that spread disinformation and can be used to launder false narratives into public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media manipulation can create compelling narratives that are repeatedly shared; verification of media provenance and forensic analysis are implied countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bots, fake accounts, and click farms creating false consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated accounts and coordinated inauthentic behavior 'pretend to be people they're not and create a false sense of consensus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kornbluh and Goodman: these actors amplify messages to manufacture engagement and apparent popular support. Detection can include bot analysis, account network mapping, and anomaly detection in engagement patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform algorithmic incentives (engagement over truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial platforms designed to keep users online privilege engagement over truth or public interest; algorithms reward outrage and disgust, which fuels spread of laundered content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding platform incentives helps explain why emotionally charged, low-veracity material spreads; mitigation requires platform-level policy and design changes as well as editorial vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: State actor cyber-amplification and forged materials
rubrics_metrics.description: State actors engaging in information laundering are supported by cyber capabilities that enhance spread and amplification, e.g., creating fake personas, burner accounts, and distributing forged letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NATO and other reports cite Russia and other states using coordinated technical and human resources to amplify laundered content. Indicators include synchronized amplification, cross-platform fake personas, and distribution of forged documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI and synthetic content to disguise origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial intelligence (generative AI) is used to launder articles (e.g., translating state media into local languages) and to create seemingly-authentic affiliate sites that hide the original source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphika and other reports describe CGTN affiliates using generative AI to translate and republish content without origin indication. Watch for multiple sites publishing translated copies with no clear attribution and for patterns of automated translation/publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactured personas and deceptive bylines
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation and use of fabricated authors or commentators (manufactured personas) to present state narratives as organic sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. Department of State example: the fictitious columnist 'Yi Fan' used to present pro-state views. Indicators include repeated bylines with no verifiable biography, cross-promotion of the same persona across platforms, and coordination between persona output and official narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party site laundering and affiliate networks
rubrics_metrics.description: State or organizational media content is republished through third-party or seemingly independent websites (affiliate networks) to mask origin and imply broader grassroots support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include state media content being run on ostensibly independent local sites which are then cited by other outlets. Detection involves tracing publishing networks, domain registrations, and content similarity across sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hijacking real-world causes and events to launder narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Using genuine local events or causes (e.g., charity rallies) to insert laundered narratives so they receive mainstream local coverage and appear authentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: QAnon's appropriation of 'Save the Children' rallies to attract local TV coverage. Monitor whether organizers or messages align with external networks or narratives rather than grassroots stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation laundering and idea laundering (scholarly/academic variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices in academia where ideas or claims are recycled through citations (self-citation, citation farms, or hidden plagiarism) that increase apparent authority without rigorous sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation laundering includes hiding a self-citation by citing an intermediary, citing recent works that all trace to one flawed source, and forming citation farms/cartels. This increases seeming authority of claims and can create academic-style laundering of dubious ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators for detection and tooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts and tools exist to uncover republishing and laundering patterns, e.g., open-source tools released to detect websites republishing content from state media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2024 example: a joint open-source tool from the Alliance for Securing Democracy, University of Amsterdam, and Institute for Strategic Dialogue. Detection guidance implicitly includes tracking cross-posting, source attribution, temporal patterns, and network amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversarial machine learning definition (model-protection context)
rubrics_metrics.description: In adversarial machine learning, 'information laundering' refers to deliberately altering information released to adversaries to alleviate model stealing attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a distinct, technical usage: rather than propagating disinformation, it is an intentional strategy to protect model privacy by changing observable outputs.
